title: Joshua 13:24–33
context: The chapter completes the eastern allotments with Gad, in Gilead and the Jordan valley up to the sea of Chinnereth, and the eastern half of Manasseh, in Bashan, the former kingdom of Og, with special mention of Machir’s clan. A summary ties these grants to Moses in the plains of Moab, and the chapter closes by repeating that the LORD himself is Levi’s inheritance. Both traditions read the lists constructively and as shared ground about God’s faithful provision.

verses.text: Moses gave to the tribe of Gad, to the children of Gad, according to their families.
verses.arminianNotes:
Moses gave Gad its inheritance according to its families. A new allotment begins.

Arminian readers see the same careful provision extended to Gad as to Reuben. Each tribe is treated with equal attention.
verses.reformedNotes:
The formula repeats verse 15 for Gad. The structure emphasizes order and fairness.

Reformed readers see God’s even-handed care for each tribe. Both traditions read this as shared ground, introducing another list that records God’s promise made concrete for real families and towns.

verses.text: Their border was Jazer, and all the cities of Gilead, and half the land of the children of Ammon, to Aroer that is near Rabbah;
verses.arminianNotes:
Gad’s border includes Jazer, all Gilead’s cities, and half the land of the Ammonites, to Aroer near Rabbah. This Aroer appears to be different from the one on the Arnon.

Arminian readers see the details as part of a carefully recorded inheritance.
verses.reformedNotes:
The territory moves north and east of Reuben. Rabbah was the Ammonite capital.

Reformed readers see God’s gift extending into contested regions. Both traditions read this as shared ground, noting that Judges 11:12–27 later records a dispute over this region, in which Jephthah argues that Israel took it from Sihon.

verses.text: and from Heshbon to Ramath Mizpeh, and Betonim; and from Mahanaim to the border of Debir;
verses.arminianNotes:
From Heshbon to Ramath Mizpeh and Betonim, and from Mahanaim to the border of Debir. This Debir is usually distinguished from the better-known town in Judah.

Arminian readers see a defined region where Gad can settle securely.
verses.reformedNotes:
Mahanaim recalls Jacob’s encounter with angels (Genesis 32:1–2). Old memories mark the land.

Reformed readers see continuity between the patriarchs and the tribes. Both traditions read this as shared ground, with caution about the exact locations of some names.

verses.text: and in the valley, Beth Haram, Beth Nimrah, Succoth, and Zaphon, the rest of the kingdom of Sihon king of Heshbon, the Jordan’s bank, to the uttermost part of the sea of Chinnereth beyond the Jordan eastward.
verses.arminianNotes:
In the valley, Beth Haram, Beth Nimrah, Succoth, and Zaphon, with the rest of Sihon’s kingdom along the Jordan to the sea of Chinnereth. The sea is usually identified with the Sea of Galilee.

Arminian readers see the Jordan valley included in Gad’s portion.
verses.reformedNotes:
Succoth also appears in Jacob’s story (Genesis 33:17). The list follows the river north.

Reformed readers see God’s gift covering fertile land. Both traditions read this as shared ground, holding identifications cautiously.

verses.text: This is the inheritance of the children of Gad according to their families, the cities and its villages.
verses.arminianNotes:
This is Gad’s inheritance by families, with cities and villages. The section closes with the usual formula.

Arminian readers see another tribe settled in God’s provision. What was promised to Gad has now been given.
verses.reformedNotes:
The summary marks the completion of Gad’s allotment. The repetition stresses that each tribe received what God intended.

Reformed readers see God’s faithfulness to every tribe. Both traditions read this as shared ground, and both see these closing formulas as small confessions of God’s faithfulness to his promise.

verses.text: Moses gave an inheritance to the half-tribe of Manasseh. It was for the half-tribe of the children of Manasseh according to their families.
verses.arminianNotes:
Moses gave an inheritance to the half-tribe of Manasseh by families. The third eastern group is introduced.

Arminian readers see the divided tribe still fully provided for on both sides of the Jordan.
verses.reformedNotes:
Manasseh is split between east and west. The eastern half receives its portion here.

Reformed readers see God’s provision reaching each part of his people. Both traditions read this as shared ground, and Numbers 32:33–42 tells how this eastern settlement began.

verses.text: Their border was from Mahanaim, all Bashan, all the kingdom of Og king of Bashan, and all the villages of Jair, which are in Bashan, sixty cities.
verses.arminianNotes:
Their border runs from Mahanaim through all Bashan and Og’s kingdom, including the villages of Jair, sixty cities. Elsewhere Bashan is associated with fine cattle and oaks (Amos 4:1; Isaiah 2:13).

Arminian readers see good land given to those who had trusted God’s promise.
verses.reformedNotes:
The sixty cities of Jair echo Deuteronomy 3:4 and 3:14. Og’s former kingdom becomes an inheritance.

Reformed readers see God turning a formidable enemy’s land into a gift. Both traditions read this as shared ground and a sign of God’s generosity.

verses.text: Half Gilead, Ashtaroth, and Edrei, the cities of the kingdom of Og in Bashan, were for the children of Machir the son of Manasseh, even for the half of the children of Machir according to their families.
verses.arminianNotes:
Half Gilead, Ashtaroth, and Edrei go to the descendants of Machir son of Manasseh. Machir’s clan is singled out.

Arminian readers see family lines honored in the distribution of the land.
verses.reformedNotes:
Machir’s descendants receive Og’s royal cities. Numbers 32:39–40 records Machir’s role in taking Gilead.

Reformed readers see God rewarding faithful action within the bounds of his promise. Both traditions read this as shared ground and note the continuing importance of clan identity in Israel.

verses.text: These are the inheritances which Moses distributed in the plains of Moab, beyond the Jordan at Jericho, eastward.
verses.arminianNotes:
These are the inheritances Moses distributed in the plains of Moab beyond the Jordan at Jericho. The eastern allotments are summarized.

Arminian readers see Moses’ work completed and honored before Joshua divides the west.
verses.reformedNotes:
The summary ties the eastern allotments to Moses’ final days in Moab. Joshua builds on that foundation.

Reformed readers see continuity in God’s plan across leaders. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s faithfulness from one generation to the next.

verses.text: But Moses gave no inheritance to the tribe of Levi. The LORD, the God of Israel, is their inheritance, as he spoke to them.
verses.arminianNotes:
Moses gave Levi no inheritance; the LORD, the God of Israel, is their inheritance, as he said. The chapter ends on this note.

Arminian readers see a reminder that God himself is the greatest portion for those who serve him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Verse 14 spoke of the offerings; here the LORD himself is their inheritance. The two statements belong together.

Reformed readers see in Levi’s portion an image of every believer’s hope, echoed in Psalm 16:5 and 73:26. Both traditions share this reading.
